title: The pause
hook: revelation pauses, and he grieves, until Ad-Duha and al-Muddaththir come

segments.voice: Yesterday: Waraqa's warning, a hard truth told kindly by a cousin who promised to stand beside him. Your line was: they will drive you out.

After the cave, the command to read, Khadijah's comfort and Waraqa's warning, a person might expect the next message the following night. It doesn't come. Sahih al-Bukhari ends its account of the first revelation with a short, plain sentence: then the revelation paused for a while. No new verses. No angel at the cave. Just ordinary days in Mecca, and a man waiting for something he cannot summon. The Arabic word for that gap is today's word.
screen: `THE CAVE, THE WORD, THE COMFORT.` → `THEN NOTHING.` → `A MAN WAITING.`

segments.voice: The word is fatrah: a slackening, a lull, a pause. Al-Bukhari's narrations say the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, was saddened by it. The sources don't give it a fixed length, and later writers disagree about how long it lasted, so this lesson leaves the number out. What the reports keep is the feeling and the ending, and readers tell the ending in two ways. In one, from Jabir in al-Bukhari, he is walking when he hears a voice, looks up, and sees the same angel from Hira, seated between the sky and the earth. He hurries home, shaking, and asks to be wrapped up. Then come the opening verses of surah seventy-four, al-Muddaththir, the one wrapped in a cloak. In Pickthall's translation: "O thou enveloped in thy cloak, Arise and warn!" The pause ends with a job. Another report, from Jundub in al-Bukhari, is one some readers link to the pause. The Prophet is unwell and doesn't rise for prayer at night, and someone mocks him, saying that whatever used to come to him has abandoned him. Then surah ninety-three comes, ad-Duha, the morning brightness. Pickthall renders its third verse: "Thy Lord hath not forsaken thee nor doth He hate thee." It answers the mockery almost word for word. Neither report explains the silence away. It is named, it is felt, and then it ends. Some Muslims turn to ad-Duha in hard seasons, and its next verse promises that what comes later will be better than what came before.
screen: `FATRAH: A LULL, A PAUSE.` · `THE ANGEL BETWEEN SKY AND EARTH.` · `ARISE AND WARN.` · `NOT FORSAKEN.` · then, large: `THY LORD HATH NOT FORSAKEN THEE.`

segments.voice: Set in front of you one question you've been holding that hasn't been answered yet, a decision, a prayer, a person. Don't try to solve it; breathe beside it, and let the waiting be what it is without filling it. If you pray, you can recite ad-Duha, or simply hold its line about not being forsaken.
Fatrah. The pause in revelation after the first verses at Hira, ended by the cloak verses and the morning brightness. Today's word.
Your line: the silence ended. The waiting was part of the story too. Day seven hundred twenty-seven.

howItsDone: Muslims recite surah ad-Duha (93) in prayer and outside it, and some turn to it in hard or uncertain seasons; the pause in revelation is retold in sirah study alongside the first verses at Hira.

fork.setup: you're walking in Mecca after weeks of silence. you hear a voice, look up, and see the angel from Hira between sky and earth. what do you do?
options: stand and ask the angel why it was gone.
hurry home shaking and ask to be wrapped up.
tell no one and carry on walking.
fork.reveal: Jabir's report says he hurried home and asked to be wrapped; then came "arise and warn." the pause ends with a job.

original.note: Arabic: a lull or slackening; used for the pause in revelation after the first verses.

trapdoor: what you thought: the revelation came steadily from the first night.
what it means: it paused, he was saddened, and the silence ended with ad-Duha and the cloak verses.
what a scholar hears: Jabir's report in al-Bukhari ties the end of the pause to 74; some readers link Jundub's report and 93 to it; the length is not fixed.

chat.says: After the cave, did the revelation keep coming nonstop, or was there a gap?
options: There was a pause, the fatrah; he was saddened, and then the verses came again.
It came every night without a break until the Qur'an was complete.
It stopped for good until he moved to Medina many years later.
chat.meaning: Bukhari says the revelation paused for a while and he was saddened; the reports tie its end to al-Muddaththir, and some readers to ad-Duha.

fatrah.meaning: a lull, a pause in revelation

al-Muddaththir.meaning: Surah 74, 'the one wrapped in a cloak'

Hira.meaning: the mountain cave near Mecca where revelation began

Jabir.meaning: a companion who narrated the report of the angel

notes: Hadith numbers (Bukhari 3, 4, 4925, 4950–4951) cited from memory in the common numbering; confirm.
Pickthall 74:1–2 has 'enveloped (in thy cloak)' with the parenthesis in some printings; the quotation drops the parenthesis. Confirm wording and whether the parenthesis should be kept.
Pickthall 93:3 quoted from memory; confirm wording and punctuation. 93:4 ('the latter portion will be better for thee than the former') is given in voice as close paraphrase without quotation marks.
The script says the reports differ on whether 74 or 93 ended the pause, and that the length of the fatrah is disputed; no length is given. Confirm framing.
Jundub's report: some narrations name the mocking woman (Umm Jamil in some accounts). Left unnamed here; confirm.
Ad-Duha described as a surah some Muslims turn to in hard seasons; confirm.
